results.finding: In regular drinkers (10 or more standard drinks a week) with paroxysmal or persistent AF, abstinence for 6 months reduced AF recurrence (53% vs 73%) and AF burden compared with usual drinking.
results.source: Voskoboinik A, Kalman JM, De Silva A, et al. Alcohol abstinence in drinkers with atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med 2020;382:20-28

results.finding: Stroke risk is assessed with CHA2DS2-VA; oral anticoagulation is recommended at a score of 2 or more and considered at 1; it is not indicated at 0. Reducing alcohol and weight are part of risk-factor management to reduce AF recurrence.
results.source: Van Gelder IC, Rienstra M, Bunting KV, et al. 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation. Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314-3414

output.summary: Alcohol abstinence reduces AF recurrence in regular drinkers; ESC 2024 bases anticoagulation on CHA2DS2-VA and includes alcohol and weight reduction in AF risk-factor management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Three witnessed dysphasic episodes building over 8-10 min, lasting 15-25 min, each followed by headache; 4 of 6 C characteristics; isolated aphasic aura and AF flagged; CHA2DS2-VA 0 without the episodes; normal examination
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and SNNOOP10 red-flag review, applying each ICHD-3 1.2 criterion
action_criteria.rationale: The history carries the diagnosis (gradual build-up, duration, headache after each episode, stereotyped recurrence) and frames the question the work-up must answer: are the episodes aura or cardioembolic TIAs in a man with paroxysmal AF. The answer also decides anticoagulation, since TIA would raise CHA2DS2-VA from 0 to 2.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute or old cortical or territorial infarct; a few non-specific frontal white matter foci
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI with DWI for isolated aphasic episodes in a patient with paroxysmal AF
action_criteria.rationale: An isolated aphasic aura and a documented embolic source are red flags (AHS neuroimaging evidence assessment, Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336); silent cortical or territorial infarcts would point to embolism. Recommended rather than required because the clinical features are those of aura.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No intracranial or cervical arterial stenosis, occlusion or dissection
action_criteria.label: MR angiography of the head and neck to exclude large-artery disease
action_criteria.rationale: Recurrent focal episodes in one territory raise large-artery stenosis or dissection as an alternative embolic source; vessel imaging completes the ischaemic work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Nocturnal paroxysmal AF; a symptomatic daytime episode recorded in sinus rhythm with no AF in the preceding 24 hours
action_criteria.label: Implantable loop recorder to correlate the aphasic episodes with the heart rhythm
action_criteria.rationale: AF is already known; the question is symptom-rhythm correlation. With episodes every 6-7 weeks, only prolonged monitoring can capture one, and an episode in sinus rhythm with no preceding AF dissociates the two conditions.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: NSAID with a DOAC increases bleeding risk; paracetamol or a triptan can be used while anticoagulated
action_criteria.label: Check his ibuprofen use and the acute migraine options against apixaban
action_criteria.rationale: Required: he takes ibuprofen 400-600 mg for each headache while on apixaban, a concrete interaction that changes his acute treatment until the anticoagulation decision is made.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on alcohol abstinence in AF and on CHA2DS2-VA thresholds
action_criteria.label: Literature on alcohol and AF recurrence and on anticoagulation at low stroke risk
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step in the patient's pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the aphasic episodes to AF: the loop recorder shows a symptomatic episode in sinus rhythm.
Do not exclude migraine with aura because AF is present: the two conditions coexist.
Do not take ibuprofen or other NSAIDs while on apixaban.
required_recommendations: Explain the two diagnoses: migraine with aphasic (typical) aura, ICHD-3 1.2.1, and separate paroxysmal AF; the loop recorder shows a symptomatic episode in sinus rhythm and MRI shows no infarct, so the episodes are not cardioembolic.
Stop apixaban after review with cardiology: with the episodes attributed to aura, CHA2DS2-VA is 0 and ESC 2024 does not recommend anticoagulation.

Treat AF triggers as part of AF management: reduce or stop alcohol (abstinence reduced AF recurrence in regular drinkers, Voskoboinik 2020) and lose weight, with rate or rhythm control decided by cardiology.

Acute migraine treatment: stop ibuprofen while on apixaban and use paracetamol 1 g with an antiemetic, or a triptan at headache onset (no interaction with apixaban, no vascular contraindication); an NSAID is acceptable again once apixaban is stopped.
Keep a headache diary; prevention is not indicated at three attacks in five months.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis — neither present here

accepted: Migraine with aphasic aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) co-existing with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (alcohol-related, nocturnal); AF and aphasic episodes temporally dissociated on implantable loop recorder

differential.key_features: Loop recorder: a symptomatic episode in sinus rhythm with no AF in the preceding 24 hours, AF only at night and asymptomatic; MRI shows no cortical or territorial infarct; gradual build-up and headache after each episode are aura features.
Normal intracranial and cervical MRA; no infarct on MRI.
Preserved awareness and comprehension, 15-25 minute duration and a migrainous headache after every episode argue against it.
Language-specific with preserved memory; not amnestic.

key_clinical_evidence: Two coexisting diagnoses: paroxysmal AF and migraine with aphasic aura; symptom-rhythm correlation on the loop recorder separates them.
Aphasia is a typical aura symptom and counts as unilateral (ICHD-3); gradual build-up, 15-25 minute duration and headache after each episode give 4 of 6 C characteristics.
Without the episodes, CHA2DS2-VA is 0: ESC 2024 does not recommend anticoagulation, so the apixaban started for presumed TIA risk is stopped with cardiology.
NSAIDs with a DOAC increase bleeding risk; paracetamol or a triptan are the acute options while he remains anticoagulated.
Alcohol at 12-15 units a week is a modifiable AF trigger; abstinence reduces recurrence (Voskoboinik 2020).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The Holter runs were asymptomatic; the loop recorder shows AF only at night and a symptomatic episode in sinus rhythm with no AF in the preceding 24 hours, and MRI shows no infarct. AF is comorbid, not causal, and his own CHA2DS2-VA is 0.
red_herrings.data_point: Paroxysmal AF found on Holter after the second episode, apixaban started
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors on cardioembolic TIA as the cause of the aphasic episodes and on continuing anticoagulation

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history is not part of CHA2DS2-VA; his own score is 0 once the episodes are recognised as aura.
red_herrings.data_point: Father had AF and a stroke at 67
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises the perceived stroke risk and the case for anticoagulation

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Punctate frontal subcortical foci without restricted diffusion, cortical involvement or lacunes are non-specific and common in migraine with aura; they are not embolic infarcts.
red_herrings.intended_effect: May be read as embolic or small-vessel ischaemic lesions supporting TIA

sequence_constraints.reason: The structured history identifies the red flags (isolated aphasic aura, embolic source) that justify imaging.
MRI evidence of infarction would settle the embolic question and the anticoagulation decision before an invasive loop recorder is implanted.

findings.result: Three stereotyped episodes in 5 months. Occasional flickering lights lasting a few minutes over 3 years, never assessed.

Speech and language: word-finding failure and paraphasic errors with preserved comprehension, witnessed by his wife in two episodes. No visual, sensory, motor or brainstem symptoms during these episodes.
Builds up over 8-10 min, peaks, clears over 5-10 min; total 15-25 min; full recovery.
Follows each episode: right-sided, throbbing, severe, with nausea and photophobia, lasting 10-16 h. Treated with ibuprofen 400-600 mg.

Paroxysmal AF found on a GP 24-hour Holter after the second episode (three asymptomatic runs of 8-22 min); apixaban 5 mg twice daily started then. No palpitations reported during the language episodes.
Normal language and neurological examination; regular pulse 76; BP 132/82 mmHg; no carotid bruit.

Isolated aphasic aura: present. New headache pattern: present. Potential embolic source (paroxysmal AF): present. Systemic symptoms, neoplasm history, deficit outside the episodes, thunderclap onset, onset over 50, positional features, papilloedema, painful eye, trauma and medication overuse: absent.
Mother had migraine with visual aura; father had AF and a stroke at 67.

clinical_assessment.impression: 1. Three attacks fulfilling ICHD-3 1.2 criteria A-C (4 of 6 C characteristics; aphasia counts as unilateral): the clinical features are those of migraine with typical (aphasic) aura, ICHD-3 1.2.1. 2. Red flags present: isolated aphasic aura and a documented embolic source; criterion D depends on excluding cardioembolic and other ischaemic causes. 3. Normal examination.

scores.CHA2DS2-VA (ESC 2024), excluding the epi: 0 (age under 65, no heart failure, hypertension, diabetes, stroke or TIA, or vascular disease)
scores.ICHD-3 1.2 criterion C characteristics m: 4 of 6 (spread, 5-60 min duration, unilateral, headache within 60 min; no positive symptom, no succession)

alternatives: Paracetamol 1 g with an antiemetic, or a triptan, at headache onset while anticoagulated
contraindications: Apixaban: active clinically significant bleeding, lesion at high bleeding risk, severe hepatic impairment with coagulopathy.
Sumatriptan (SmPC): ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, hemiplegic migraine and migraine with brainstem aura.
interactions: Apixaban with ibuprofen or naproxen: additive bleeding risk, including gastrointestinal bleeding; avoid regular or repeated NSAID use with an anticoagulant.
Apixaban with paracetamol: no interaction at usual doses.
Apixaban with sumatriptan or other triptans: no pharmacokinetic interaction.
Apixaban with strong CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitors (azole antifungals, ritonavir) or inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort): avoid or adjust.
apixaban.proposed: acute migraine treatment against apixaban 5 mg twice daily; current ibuprofen 400-600 mg as needed
apixaban.summary: Ibuprofen with apixaban raises bleeding risk and should be avoided; paracetamol and triptans do not interact with apixaban. Sources: apixaban and sumatriptan SmPC; BNF.
warnings: Alcohol increases bleeding risk with anticoagulants and is a trigger for AF episodes.
Triptans are taken at the onset of headache, not during the aura.
Acute medication on 10 or more days a month (triptans) or 15 or more days (simple analgesics) risks medication-overuse headache.
Topiramate, propranolol and candesartan have no clinically relevant interaction with apixaban.

additional_observations: Indication: recurrent transient dysphasia; paroxysmal AF.
Technique: sagittal T1, axial T2, FLAIR, DWI with ADC and SWI.
No cortical or territorial infarct, no lacune, no microbleed.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: paroxysmal AF with aphasic episodes creates a strong TIA presumption; symptom-rhythm correlation on the loop recorder resolves it; the anticoagulation decision follows from CHA2DS2-VA once the episodes are aura; alcohol as a modifiable AF trigger

family_history: Mother had migraine with visual aura; father had AF and stroke at 67; no family history of coagulopathy

patient.history_present_illness:
A 44-year-old American businessman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic after three episodes of transient language difficulty over the past 5 months. He describes his speech becoming disorganised over several minutes — he knows what he wants to say but produces wrong words or cannot select words at all. His wife, who was present for two of the three episodes, confirms he produces paraphasic errors and cannot complete sentences but appears to understand what is said to him. Episodes begin gradually over approximately 8-10 minutes, peak, then resolve over another 5-10 minutes. Total duration 15-25 minutes. Following the language difficulty, he develops a severe right-sided throbbing headache lasting 10-16 hours, with nausea and light sensitivity.

Significantly: during the cardiac evaluation following the second episode, his GP performed a 24-hour Holter which unexpectedly revealed paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (PAF) — three brief episodes lasting 8-22 minutes. He was immediately started on apixaban 5 mg twice daily and referred to neurology to determine whether his language episodes represent cardioembolic TIA due to AF, or whether the AF is incidental.

He has no prior stroke, no cardiac history, no hypertension. He is overweight (BMI 29). He drinks 12-15 units of alcohol a week. He has a strong family history — mother had migraines with visual aura; father had AF and a stroke at 67. He is a non-smoker. He works 60-hour weeks in a high-stress financial role. He has had occasional 'flickers of light' that lasted a few minutes over the past 3 years that he did not report.
